title: Relations of Partners
outcomes: State the mutual rights and duties of partners (Sections 9 to 17), including the default rules of Section 13, and apply them to profit-distribution problems.
Explain a partner's implied authority, its extension, restriction and limits, and the effect of admissions and notice (Sections 18 to 24).
Apply the rules on liability of partners to third parties, transfer of interest and minors (Sections 25 to 30).
Analyse the consequences of admission, retirement, expulsion, insolvency and death of a partner, and the outgoing partner's rights (Sections 31 to 38).

meta.exam_tip: Section 13 problems (salary, interest, ratio), minors (Section 30), implied authority (Section 19(2)) and expulsion (Section 33) are the favourites. Quote the clause, apply to each claim, conclude.

concepts.title: Relation of partners to one another (Sections 9 to 15)
body: Section 9 — general duties: carry on the business to the greatest common advantage, be just and faithful to one another, and give true accounts and full information of everything affecting the firm to any partner or his legal representative. Utmost good faith runs through the whole relationship.

Section 10: a partner who causes loss to the firm by fraud in conducting its business must make the loss good. Section 11: partners may fix or vary their mutual rights by contract, express or implied from a course of dealing; such a contract may validly bar a partner from carrying on any other business while he is a partner, despite Section 27 of the Contract Act.

Section 12 — conduct of business (subject to contract): every partner may take part in the business and must attend diligently to his duties; ordinary differences are settled by majority after every partner has had his say, but the nature of the business cannot be changed without the consent of all; every partner — active or sleeping — may inspect and copy the books; after a partner's death his heirs or legal representatives have the same right of access.

Section 13 — mutual rights and liabilities (subject to contract): (a) no remuneration for working in the business; (b) profits shared and losses borne equally; (c) interest on capital, where payable, only out of profits; (d) interest at 6% a year on advances made beyond agreed capital; (e) indemnity by the firm for payments and liabilities in the ordinary and proper conduct of business and for prudent acts done in an emergency to protect the firm; (f) a partner must indemnify the firm for loss caused by his wilful neglect.

Sections 14–15 — property of the firm: all property brought into the common stock, all property acquired by or for the firm or for its business, and goodwill, unless the partners intend otherwise; it must be held and used exclusively for the business. Merely using a partner's own asset for the business does not make it firm property.
concepts.analogy: Section 13 is the "default settings" screen of a phone: if the partners never change the settings in their deed, these settings apply automatically.
concepts.work: When a firm has no deed (common in small businesses), a CA preparing accounts must apply the Section 13 defaults — equal shares, no salary, no interest on capital, 6% on advances — or the accounts will not reflect the legal position.

concepts.title: Personal profit (Section 16) and change in the firm (Section 17)
body: Section 16 (subject to contract): (a) any personal gain a partner makes out of the firm's dealings, or by exploiting its property, contacts or name, must be disclosed and handed over to the firm; (b) a partner who runs a business of the same nature as, and competing with, the firm must hand over all profits of that business to the firm.
Illustration: a partner entrusted with buying raw material for the firm quietly sells his own stock to the firm at market rates and keeps the margin — he must pay that profit to the firm.

Section 17 (subject to contract): when the constitution of the firm changes (a partner joins or leaves), the mutual rights and duties continue as before, as far as may be; when a fixed-term firm carries on after the term, rights continue so far as consistent with a partnership at will; when a firm formed for one venture takes up further ventures, the same rights and duties apply to the new ones.
concepts.analogy: A partner is like a trustee of the firm's opportunities: he cannot pocket a side profit he earned only because he wore the firm's badge.
concepts.work: Forensic and internal-audit assignments in firms often uncover related-party purchases routed through a partner. Section 16 is the legal basis for recovering such secret profits.

concepts.title: Partner as agent: implied authority and its limits (Sections 18 to 22)
body: Section 18: for the purpose of the firm's business, a partner is its agent. Section 19(1): when a partner does something in the ordinary manner of the trade the firm is engaged in, the firm is bound — this is his "implied authority". Section 22: the act must be done in the firm name or in a way showing an intention to bind the firm.
Section 19(2): unless trade usage or custom says otherwise, implied authority does not cover eight acts — see the table. The firm is not bound by such acts unless the other partners authorise them.
Implied authority varies with the business: drawing a promissory note may be usual for a banking firm but not for a firm of lawyers.

Section 20: partners may extend or restrict implied authority by contract (all partners must agree). An act beyond a restriction still binds the firm unless the third party knew of the restriction or did not know he was dealing with a partner. Section 21: in an emergency a partner may do whatever a person of ordinary prudence would do in his own case to protect the firm from loss, and it binds the firm.

blocks.title: Implied authority of a partner

concepts.analogy: Implied authority is a "standard key card" every partner carries: it opens the ordinary doors of the business. Eight rooms (Section 19(2)) need a special key from all partners.
concepts.work: Banks insist on a partnership letter signed by all partners before opening an account or accepting a mortgage, precisely because these acts may fall outside one partner's implied authority.

concepts.title: Admissions (Section 23) and notice to acting partner (Section 24)
body: Section 23: an admission or representation made by a partner about the firm's affairs, in the ordinary course of business, is evidence against the firm. It will not bind the firm where the partner's authority on that point was restricted and the other side knew it; and between partners themselves it is not conclusive.

Section 24: notice to a partner who habitually acts in the firm's business, on a matter relating to the firm's affairs, operates as notice to the firm — except where a fraud on the firm is committed by, or with the consent of, that partner. The notice must be actual, received by a working (not sleeping) partner, and concern the firm's business.
concepts.analogy: Telling the duty manager is telling the shop — unless the duty manager is the one cheating the shop.
concepts.work: Legal notices, GST notices and customer complaints received by the managing partner are treated as received by the firm. CAs advise firms to log such notices centrally so deadlines are not missed.

concepts.title: Liability to third parties (Sections 25 to 28)
body: Section 25: each partner answers for every act of the firm done during his time as partner — together with the others (jointly) and on his own (severally). Under Section 2(a), an "act of a firm" covers anything done or omitted by the partners, by one partner, or by an agent of the firm, which creates a legally enforceable right for or against the firm.

Section 26: if a partner, while doing the firm's ordinary business or acting with his co-partners' authority, commits a wrong that harms an outsider, the firm is answerable for it just as much as that partner.

Section 27: the firm must compensate an outsider whose money or property is misused by a partner, whether (a) the partner took it from the outsider while apparently authorised to do so, or (b) the firm took it in the course of business and a partner misused it while the firm held it.
Section 28: a person who holds himself out (or lets himself be held out) as a partner is liable to those who gave credit to the firm relying on it (see Unit 1).
concepts.analogy: In a firm, one partner's signature is everyone's signature, and one partner's mistake at work is everyone's mistake.
concepts.work: Because liability is joint and several, a creditor can recover the whole debt from any one partner. CAs advising partners on personal guarantees and asset protection start from Section 25.

concepts.title: Transferee of a partner's interest (Section 29)
body: A partner may sell, mortgage or otherwise transfer his interest, but the transferee does not become a partner (that needs the consent of all partners — Section 31).

While the firm continues, the transferee cannot interfere in the business, demand accounts or inspect the books. He is entitled only to the transferring partner's share of profits and must accept the profits as agreed by the partners.

On dissolution, or on the retirement of the transferring partner, he may claim against the remaining partners the share of assets the transferor was entitled to, and an account from the date of dissolution to work it out.
concepts.analogy: Buying a partner's interest is like buying a ticket to the profits — not a seat in the driver's cabin.
concepts.work: Partners often pledge their partnership interest to raise personal loans. A CA must explain to the lender that it gets profit rights and dissolution rights only, not management or inspection rights.

concepts.title: Minors admitted to the benefits of partnership (Section 30)
body: A minor cannot be a partner because his agreement is void, but with the consent of all partners he may be admitted to the benefits of an existing partnership.

Within six months of attaining majority, or of first learning that he was admitted to benefits (whichever is later), he must decide whether to become a partner and may give public notice of his choice. Silence for six months makes him a partner.

If he becomes a partner he is personally liable for all acts of the firm since his original admission to benefits, and his share stays the same. If he elects not to, his share is not liable for acts after the date of the public notice.

blocks.title: Minor admitted to the benefits of partnership — Section 30

concepts.analogy: A minor in a firm is a passenger with a ticket to the profits; at 18 he gets six months to decide whether to become a crew member — and crew members answer for the whole voyage.
concepts.work: Families often admit children to the benefits of the family firm. CAs must diarise the child's 18th birthday: a missed six-month window can make the child personally liable for years of past debts.

concepts.title: Partner coming in and going out (Sections 31 to 35)
body: Section 31: no new partner can be brought in without the consent of all existing partners (subject to contract and to Section 30). He is not liable for acts done before he joined unless he agrees; making him liable to old creditors needs the creditors' agreement (novation).

Section 32: a partner may retire with the consent of all the others, under an express agreement, or, in a partnership at will, by written notice to all the others. He can be discharged from liability for acts before retirement by agreement with the third party and the reconstituted firm (express or implied from dealings). He and the others remain liable for acts that would be acts of the firm until public notice of retirement is given — but not to a person who dealt with the firm without knowing he was a partner. Notice may be given by him or by any partner of the reconstituted firm.

Section 33: expulsion by a majority is valid only if the power exists in the contract and is exercised in good faith — in the firm's interest, after notice to the partner and a chance to be heard. Otherwise the expulsion is void. Rules on liability of a retired partner apply to an expelled partner.

Section 34: an insolvent partner ceases to be a partner from the date of the adjudication order, whether or not the firm is dissolved; where the firm continues, neither side answers for the other's acts done after the order — his estate is free of the firm's later acts and the firm is free of his.
Section 35: where the firm continues after a partner's death, his estate is not liable for acts done after the death; no public notice is needed.

head: Event
Section
Key rule
rows: Admission
Needs consent of all existing partners; new partner not liable for acts before admission unless he agrees; creditors must agree (novation) to make him liable for old debts
Retirement

With consent of all, under an express agreement, or (at will) by written notice to all; liable to third parties for later acts till public notice; old debts discharged only by agreement with creditor and reconstituted firm
Expulsion
Only if the contract gives the power, exercised by a majority, in good faith (interest of firm, notice, chance to be heard); otherwise void
Insolvency
Ceases to be a partner from the date of the adjudication order; no liability either way for acts after that date
Death
Estate not liable for acts of the firm after death; no public notice needed
blocks.title: Partner coming in and going out — Sections 31 to 35

concepts.analogy: Joining a firm is boarding a moving train: you are not responsible for the stations already passed. Leaving it means announcing at the platform (public notice) — otherwise people think you are still on board.
concepts.work: On every admission or retirement a CA prepares the revaluation, the new deed, the public notice and the intimation to the Registrar, bank and GST authorities. Missing the public notice keeps the retiring partner exposed.

concepts.title: Outgoing partner: competing business, subsequent profits, guarantees (Sections 36 to 38)
body: Section 36: an outgoing partner may carry on a competing business and advertise it, but (subject to contract) he may not use the firm name, represent himself as carrying on the firm's business, or solicit the custom of persons who dealt with the firm before he left. He may validly agree not to carry on a similar business within a specified period or local limits, if the restrictions are reasonable (an exception to Section 27 of the Contract Act).

Section 37: where a partner dies or otherwise leaves and the others carry on the business with the firm's property without settling accounts, the outgoing partner or his estate may choose either (a) the part of the later profits that was earned with his share of the property, or (b) simple interest at 6% a year on the value of his share. If the deed gives the others an option to buy his interest and they duly exercise it, he gets no further share of profits.

Section 38: unless the parties agree otherwise, any change in the firm's constitution ends a continuing guarantee — whether given to the firm or to an outsider for the firm's dealings — for all transactions after the change.

Working
Amount (₹)

(b) Interest @ 6% p.a. on her share
blocks.title: Leela's choice for 1 October 2025 – 31 March 2026

concepts.analogy: Section 37 is a "rent or share" choice: the continuing partners are using the outgoing partner's money, so he can take either a share of what it earned or a fixed 6% rent on it.
concepts.work: Banks review guarantees every time a firm is reconstituted, because Section 38 revokes a continuing guarantee for future transactions. A CA should alert clients to obtain fresh guarantees.

illustrations.title: Distributing profit when there is no deed (Section 13)
illustrations.q: Gopal, Hari and Ishaan are partners with capitals of ₹5,00,000, ₹3,00,000 and ₹2,00,000. There is no partnership agreement. On 1 July 2025 Hari advanced ₹2,00,000 to the firm over and above his capital. Gopal, who manages the shop, claims a salary of ₹5,000 a month; Ishaan claims 10% interest on capital and wants profits shared in the capital ratio. Profit for the year ended 31 March 2026, before any of these items, is ₹3,15,000. Settle the disputes and show the distribution.

solution.provision: Section 13, applicable in the absence of a contract: (a) no partner is entitled to remuneration for taking part in the business; (b) partners share profits equally; (c) interest on capital, where payable, is payable only out of profits — and is payable only if agreed; (d) a partner who advances money beyond his agreed capital gets interest at 6% per annum.
solution.facts: There is no agreement on salary, interest on capital or the sharing ratio. Hari advanced ₹2,00,000 on 1 July 2025.
solution.analysis: Gopal's salary claim fails (Section 13(a)). Ishaan's claims fail: no agreement for interest on capital, and profits are shared equally regardless of capital (Section 13(b)). Hari gets interest on his advance at 6% for 9 months, which is a charge against profit.
solution.conclusion: Hari receives interest of ₹9,000; the balance ₹3,06,000 is shared equally — ₹1,02,000 each. Hari's total is ₹1,11,000.

illustrations.title: Outgoing partner's option under Section 37
illustrations.q: Jaya, Kunal and Leela are partners. Leela retired on 30 September 2025. Her share in the firm's property was agreed at ₹4,00,000, but it has not been paid and accounts have not been settled. Jaya and Kunal continued the business with the firm's entire property, valued at ₹20,00,000, and earned a profit of ₹3,00,000 for the half-year to 31 March 2026. Assuming profit is earned in proportion to property used, what can Leela claim for this period?

solution.provision: Section 37: where a partner leaves and the continuing partners carry on business with the firm's property without a final settlement, the outgoing partner may, at her option, claim either the share of profits since she left that is attributable to the use of her share of the property, or interest at 6% per annum on the amount of her share — unless the deed gave the others an option to buy her share which they duly exercised.
solution.facts: Leela left on 30 September 2025; her share of ₹4,00,000 is unpaid; the business continued with all the firm's property and earned ₹3,00,000 in six months. There is no purchase option in the facts.
solution.analysis: Her share is ₹4,00,000 of ₹20,00,000, i.e. one-fifth of the property used. Option (a) gives ₹60,000; option (b) gives ₹12,000. She may choose the better one.
solution.conclusion: Leela should elect option (a) and claim ₹60,000 for the half-year, in addition to her ₹4,00,000.

illustrations.title: Partner refers a firm dispute to arbitration
illustrations.q: Om, Pia and Raj are partners in a wholesale grain business. Without consulting the others, Om agrees with a buyer to refer a quality dispute of ₹8,50,000 to an arbitrator, and also opens a bank account in his own name for collecting the firm's dues. Are Pia and Raj bound?

solution.provision: Section 19(1): what a partner does in the ordinary course of the kind of trade the firm follows binds the firm. Section 19(2): unless a trade usage or custom says otherwise, this implied authority does not let a partner send a business dispute of the firm to arbitration, or open an account for the firm in his personal name.
solution.facts: Om alone referred a firm dispute to arbitration and opened a bank account in his own name. No trade custom permitting this is shown, and the others did not authorise him.
solution.analysis: Both acts fall within the list in Section 19(2) and so lie outside Om's implied authority.
solution.conclusion: Pia and Raj (and the firm) are not bound by the arbitration agreement or by the account opened in Om's name, unless they ratify these acts.

illustrations.title: Minor who stays silent after majority
illustrations.q: Sneha was admitted to the benefits of a firm in 2021 when she was 13. She turned 18 on 1 June 2026 and knew all along that she had been admitted. She gave no public notice. In January 2027 a creditor of 2024 seeks to recover from her personal assets. Advise Sneha.

solution.provision: Section 30(5): within six months of attaining majority or of obtaining knowledge of her admission, whichever is later, a minor admitted to benefits may give public notice of whether she elects to become a partner; if she gives no notice she becomes a partner on expiry of the six months. Section 30(7): once she becomes a partner, her personal liability to outsiders reaches back to every act of the firm from the day she was first admitted to its benefits.
solution.facts: Sneha attained majority on 1 June 2026 and already knew of her admission. The six months ended on 1 December 2026 with no public notice. The creditor's debt arose in 2024, after her admission in 2021.
solution.analysis: Because she stayed silent, she became a partner on 1 December 2026. Her liability then extends back to the date of her admission to benefits in 2021, which covers the 2024 debt.
solution.conclusion: Sneha is personally liable for the 2024 debt; the creditor can proceed against her personal assets.

illustrations.title: Expulsion without power in the deed
illustrations.q: Uday, Vikas and Wasim are partners. Their deed contains no clause on expulsion. After a personal quarrel, Uday and Vikas pass a "resolution" expelling Wasim without notice. Is the expulsion valid?

solution.provision: Section 33(1): a majority can expel a partner only by using, honestly, a power that the partners' contract gives them. Good faith requires that the expulsion be in the interest of the firm, that the partner be given notice, and that he be given an opportunity of being heard.
solution.facts: The deed confers no power of expulsion. The decision was taken by a majority after a personal quarrel, without notice or hearing.
solution.analysis: The first condition — a contractual power — is missing. Even if it existed, a personal quarrel, no notice and no hearing would fail the test of good faith.
solution.conclusion: The expulsion is void. Wasim continues to be a partner with all his rights.

jobs.title: Year-end accounts of a firm with no deed
jobs.situation: A two-partner firm has no deed. One partner wants salary and interest on capital debited; the other partner had lent the firm ₹5,00,000 on 1 January.
steps: Apply Section 13: no salary, no interest on capital, profits equally.
Provide interest at 6% p.a. on the loan for 3 months (₹5,00,000 × 6% × 3/12 = ₹7,500) as a charge against profit.
Advise the partners to sign a deed if they want salary or interest — tax deductions also depend on the deed.
Record the partners' agreement in board-style minutes and get it stamped.
jobs.takeaway: Without a deed the Act decides: equal shares, no salary, no interest on capital, 6% on advances.
jobs.think: Would the 6% interest still be payable if the firm made a loss?
jobs.answer: Yes. Interest on an advance under Section 13(d) is a charge, not an appropriation of profit; unlike interest on capital, it is not limited to profits.

jobs.title: Admitting a new partner into a firm with bank borrowings
jobs.situation: A firm with a ₹2 crore working-capital loan admits a new partner. The bank asks whether the new partner is liable for the existing loan.
steps: Section 31(2): the new partner is not liable for acts before his admission unless he agrees.
If the bank wants him liable, he must sign a novation/guarantee with the bank and the firm.
Section 38: check existing continuing guarantees — they are revoked for future transactions on reconstitution; arrange fresh guarantees.
File the change with the Registrar of Firms and update the bank mandate.
jobs.takeaway: Reconstitution changes who is liable for what — paperwork with creditors must follow.
jobs.think: Is an internal clause in the new deed ("new partner shall bear old debts") enough for the bank to sue him?
jobs.answer: No. An agreement among partners alone is not novation; the creditor must be a party for the new partner to become liable to it.

jobs.title: Retiring partner's exit checklist
jobs.situation: Your client is retiring from a firm; the continuing partners will pay his dues in instalments over two years.
steps: Ensure public notice of retirement is given (Section 32(3)) and the Registrar is informed.
Get creditors to release him from old liabilities, or obtain an indemnity from the continuing partners (Section 32(2)).
Until he is paid, Section 37 entitles him to a share of profits attributable to his share or 6% interest — put the agreed rate in the retirement deed.
Negotiate any non-compete as a reasonable restriction in time and area (Section 36(2)).
jobs.takeaway: Public notice, release from old debts and a clear settlement clause protect a retiring partner.

mcqs.q: In the absence of an agreement, partners share profits:
options: Equally
In capital ratio
In the ratio of time devoted
As decided by the senior partner
mcqs.explain: Section 13(b): unless the partners agree otherwise, they share profits equally, and they contribute to losses equally too. Sharing in the capital ratio is the trap: it feels fair, but the Act ignores capital unless the deed says so. Time devoted and seniority are also irrelevant without an agreement. In practice: when a firm without a written deed splits up, partners who put in more capital are often shocked to learn that profits were legally shared equally, which is why CAs insist on a clear profit-sharing clause.
mcqs.topic: Relation of Partners to One Another

mcqs.q: A partner advances ₹1,50,000 to the firm beyond his capital on 1 August. There is no agreement on interest. Interest for the year ending 31 March is:
options: Nil
mcqs.explain: Section 13(d): a partner who advances money to the firm beyond his agreed capital gets interest at 6% a year, even without an agreement. The advance was made on 1 August, so it ran for 8 months to 31 March: ₹1,50,000 × 6% × 8/12 = ₹6,000. ₹9,000 is the trap: it charges a full year. "Nil" confuses an advance with capital, which earns no interest unless agreed. In practice: firms pay this interest through the partner's current account, and the deed usually sets the rate for income-tax purposes.
mcqs.topic: Relation of Partners to One Another

mcqs.q: Without trade usage to the contrary, which act is within a partner's implied authority in a trading firm?
options: Borrowing money for the firm's business
Submitting a dispute to arbitration
Buying immovable property for the firm
Withdrawing a suit filed by the firm
mcqs.explain: Under Section 19(1), a partner's implied authority covers acts done in the usual way to carry on the firm's business. In a trading firm, borrowing for the business is such an act. Section 19(2) withholds implied authority for listed acts, including submitting disputes to arbitration, buying immovable property, and withdrawing a suit. Arbitration is the trap because it sounds routine, but it is expressly excluded. In practice: banks lending to a firm still ask for a resolution or letter signed by all partners, to avoid disputes over authority.
mcqs.topic: Relation of Partners to Third Parties

mcqs.q: The nature of the firm's business can be changed:
options: Only with the consent of all partners
By a simple majority
By the managing partner
By two-thirds of the partners
mcqs.explain: Section 12(c): routine business matters can be settled by majority vote, but the nature of the business cannot be changed without the consent of every partner. A simple majority is the trap: it is enough for routine decisions, not for changing the business itself. Neither the managing partner nor a two-thirds vote can do it. In practice: if a firm trading in textiles wants to start real-estate dealing, the CA drafts a supplementary deed signed by all partners.
mcqs.topic: Relation of Partners to One Another

mcqs.q: A partner secretly earns a commission from a supplier on the firm's purchases. Under Section 16 he must:
options: Account for it and pay it to the firm
Keep it, as it is his personal income
Share it with the supplier
Pay it only if the deed says so expressly
mcqs.explain: Section 16(a): subject to the contract between partners, a partner who earns any profit for himself from a transaction of the firm, or from using its property, business connection or name, must account for it and pay it to the firm. A secret commission from the firm's supplier is exactly this. "Keep it as personal income" is the trap: a partner owes the firm a duty of good faith. The duty applies even if the deed is silent. In practice: forensic auditors check supplier side-payments to partners and recover them for the firm.

mcqs.q: A transferee of a partner's interest, while the firm continues, is entitled to:
options: The transferring partner's share of profits only
Take part in management
Inspect the books of account
Demand accounts from the partners
mcqs.explain: Section 29(1): while the firm continues, a person to whom a partner transfers his interest is entitled only to receive that partner's share of profits, accepting the profit figure agreed by the partners. He cannot take part in management, ask for accounts or inspect the books. Inspecting the books is the trap, because it feels like a basic right of anyone with money in the firm. In practice: when a partner assigns his share to a lender as security, the lender gets the profit share but cannot interfere in day-to-day running.
mcqs.topic: Rights of Transferee of a Partner’s Interest (Section 29)

mcqs.q: A minor admitted to benefits must elect whether to become a partner within:
options: 6 months of attaining majority or of learning of his admission, whichever is later
6 months of attaining majority, whichever is earlier
1 year of attaining majority
3 months of attaining majority
mcqs.explain: Section 30(5): a minor admitted to the benefits of partnership must, within six months of attaining majority or of learning of his admission, whichever is later, give public notice of whether he will become a partner. If he stays silent, he becomes a partner when the six months end. "Whichever is earlier" is the trap: the law gives the later date to protect him. One year and three months are wrong periods. In practice: family firms remind a minor beneficiary when he turns 18, as silence creates full partner liability.
mcqs.topic: Minors Admitted to the Benefits of Partnership (Section 30)

mcqs.q: Notice given to a sleeping partner about a firm matter:
options: Is not notice to the firm under Section 24
Is always notice to the firm
Binds only that partner and the managing partner
Is notice only if in writing
mcqs.explain: Section 24: notice to a partner who habitually acts in the business of the firm, about the firm's affairs, operates as notice to the firm (except where there is fraud). A sleeping partner does not habitually act in the business, so notice to him is not notice to the firm. "Always notice to the firm" is the trap: it ignores the "habitually acts" requirement. Written form is not the test. In practice: lenders and landlords send legal notices to the managing or working partner, so that the firm cannot later deny receiving them.
mcqs.topic: Effect of Notice to Acting Partner (Section 24)

mcqs.q: Which is NOT a condition for a valid expulsion under Section 33?
options: Approval of the Registrar of Firms
Power of expulsion in the contract between partners
Exercise of the power by a majority
Exercise in good faith
mcqs.explain: Section 33: a partner can be expelled only if the power to expel is given by the contract between partners, it is exercised by a majority of partners, and it is exercised in good faith. Approval from the Registrar of Firms is not required, and the Registrar has no such role. The trap is assuming every big change needs official approval. A change in the firm's constitution is later intimated to the Registrar, but that is not a condition for a valid expulsion. In practice: CAs draft expulsion clauses with a clear procedure, including notice and a hearing.
mcqs.topic: Legal Consequences of Partner Coming in and Going Out (Section 31 – 35)

mcqs.q: An insolvent partner ceases to be a partner:
options: From the date of the order of adjudication
From the date the petition is filed
From the date public notice is given
Only when the firm is dissolved
mcqs.explain: Section 34(1): a partner who is adjudged insolvent stops being a partner from the date of the adjudication order, whether or not the firm is dissolved. The date the petition is filed is the trap: an insolvency petition can be dismissed, so only the court's order counts. Public notice and dissolution are not required. In practice: when a partner is adjudged insolvent, the CA settles his capital account up to the adjudication date, and the firm stops treating his acts as binding from then on.
mcqs.topic: Legal Consequences of Partner Coming in and Going Out (Section 31 – 35)

mcqs.q: An outgoing partner, subject to contract, may NOT:
options: Solicit the custom of persons who dealt with the firm before he left
Carry on a competing business
Advertise his new business
Employ staff in his new business
mcqs.explain: Section 36(1): subject to a contract, an outgoing partner may carry on a competing business and advertise it. But he may not use the firm name, represent himself as carrying on the firm's business, or solicit the custom of people who dealt with the firm before he left. Carrying on a competing business is the trap: it is allowed. A deed may add a reasonable restraint under Section 36(2). In practice: when a partner leaves a CA firm and opens his own practice, he can work freely but cannot canvass the old firm's clients.
mcqs.topic: Rights of Outgoing Partner to Carry on Competing Business (Section 36)

mcqs.q: A continuing guarantee given to a firm, on a change in its constitution, is:
options: Revoked as to future transactions from the date of the change
Revoked for past and future transactions
Unaffected
Revoked only if the guarantor gives notice
mcqs.explain: Section 38: a continuing guarantee in favour of a firm, or to a third party covering the firm's dealings, stops covering future transactions once the firm's constitution changes, unless agreed otherwise. Past transactions remain covered. "Revoked for past and future transactions" is the trap: the guarantor remains liable for debts already incurred. No notice from the guarantor is needed. In practice: when a partner joins or retires, banks take fresh guarantees from guarantors so that new borrowings remain secured.
mcqs.topic: Revocation of Continuing Guarantee by Change in Firm (Section 38)

mcqs.q: A retired partner remains liable to third parties for acts of the firm done after his retirement until:
options: Public notice of the retirement is given
He sells his share
The firm is registered again
Six months have passed
mcqs.explain: Section 32(3): a retired partner and the continuing partners remain liable to third parties for acts that would have been acts of the firm, done before public notice of the retirement is given. After public notice, he is free of such liability. Selling his share is the trap: it settles matters with the other partners, not with outsiders. There is no automatic six-month period. In practice: a retiring partner should get the firm to publish a notice in a newspaper and file the change with the Registrar of Firms.
mcqs.topic: Legal Consequences of Partner Coming in and Going Out (Section 31 – 35)

mcqs.q: Partners are liable for acts of the firm:
options: Jointly and severally
Only jointly
Only severally
In their capital ratio only
mcqs.explain: Section 25: every partner is liable, jointly with all the other partners and also severally, for every act of the firm during his time as a partner. So a creditor may sue all the partners together or any one of them for the whole debt. "Only jointly" is the trap: it would force the creditor to sue everyone together. Capital ratio matters only for sharing among partners, not towards creditors. In practice: banks lending to firms often recover from whichever partner has the most personal assets, and that partner then claims contribution from the others.
mcqs.topic: Relation of Partners to Third Parties

questions.q: Mohan and Nikhil are partners without any written agreement. Their capitals are ₹4,00,000 and ₹6,00,000. Nikhil lent ₹3,00,000 to the firm on 1 October 2025. Mohan claims a salary of ₹5,000 per month for managing the business. Nikhil claims interest on capital at 8% and wants profits shared in the capital ratio. The profit for the year ended 31 March 2026, before any of these claims, is ₹2,49,000. Decide the claims under the Indian Partnership Act, 1932 and show the distribution.

model.text: Provision — Section 13 (applicable in the absence of a contract): (a) no remuneration for taking part in the business; (b) profits shared equally; (c) interest on capital only if agreed, and then only out of profits; (d) interest at 6% p.a. on advances beyond capital.

items: Nikhil's interest on capital at 8%: not allowed — no agreement, Section 13(c).
Sharing in capital ratio: not allowed — profits are shared equally, Section 13(b).
Interest on Nikhil's loan: allowed at 6% p.a. for 6 months = ₹9,000 — Section 13(d).

questions.q: Explain the rights and liabilities of a minor admitted to the benefits of partnership (a) before attaining majority and (b) after attaining majority.

model.text: Section 30: a minor cannot be a partner but may, with the consent of all partners, be admitted to the benefits of partnership.

items: (a) Before majority — rights: agreed share of property and profits; access to inspect and copy the accounts; may sue for his share only when severing his connection with the firm. Liability: limited to his share in the firm's property and profits; no personal liability; cannot be declared insolvent (his share vests in the official assignee if the firm is adjudged insolvent).

(b) After majority — within 6 months of majority or of knowledge of admission, whichever is later, he must elect. If he becomes a partner (by choice or by silence), he is personally liable for all acts of the firm since his admission to benefits and his share remains the same. If he elects not to and gives public notice, his rights and liabilities are those of a minor up to the notice, his share is not liable for later acts, and he may sue the partners for his share.

scheme.pt: Minor cannot be partner; admission to benefits with consent of all
Liability before majority — share only, no personal liability
Six-month election rule and effect of silence
Position on becoming / not becoming a partner

remarks: The six-month rule and the retrospective liability are tested most often.
mistakes: Saying the minor becomes liable only from the date of majority.
Saying silence means he is out of the firm.
tips: Use two headings: "Before majority" and "After majority".

questions.q: Ananya, Bhavesh and Charu are partners. The deed allows expulsion of a partner "by majority, for conduct harmful to the firm". Bhavesh is found diverting the firm's customers to his brother's business. Ananya and Charu call a meeting, give Bhavesh written notice of the charge, hear his explanation and then expel him. Bhavesh challenges the expulsion. Decide.

model.provision: Section 33(1): a partner may be expelled by a majority only in the exercise, in good faith, of a power conferred by contract between the partners. Good faith means the expulsion is in the interest of the firm, the partner is given notice, and he is given an opportunity to be heard.
model.facts: The deed confers a power of expulsion by majority for harmful conduct. Bhavesh diverted customers. Two of three partners acted after written notice and a hearing.
model.analysis: All three conditions are met: contractual power, exercise by majority, good faith (firm's interest, notice and hearing).
model.conclusion: The expulsion is valid. Bhavesh is treated like a retired partner for liability purposes under Section 33(2).

scheme.pt: Meaning of good faith — interest, notice, hearing

remarks: Show every condition being satisfied — examiners look for the three-part test.
mistakes: Stating that expulsion always needs unanimous consent.
tips: Tick off each condition in the analysis paragraph.

questions.q: What is meant by the implied authority of a partner? State the acts that are outside a partner's implied authority in the absence of usage or custom of trade.

model.text: Implied authority (Sections 19(1) and 22): the firm is bound by what a partner does in the ordinary course of the type of business the firm runs, provided it is done in the firm name or in a manner showing an intention to bind the firm. Its scope depends on the nature of the business and may be extended or restricted by agreement (Section 20).
Acts outside implied authority (Section 19(2)), unless usage or custom permits:

items: submitting a dispute relating to the firm's business to arbitration;
opening an account for the firm in his personal name;
compromising or relinquishing any claim or part of a claim of the firm;
withdrawing a case the firm has filed;
admitting any liability in a suit or proceeding against the firm;
acquiring immovable property on behalf of the firm;
transferring immovable property belonging to the firm;
entering into partnership on behalf of the firm.

scheme.pt: Meaning of implied authority with Sections 19(1) and 22
Any eight restricted acts (½ mark each)

remarks: Most candidates remember five or six acts; learn all eight with a memory hook.
mistakes: Including "borrowing money" or "buying goods" in the restricted list.
tips: Hook: "A-B-C-W-A-I-T-E" — Arbitration, Bank account, Compromise, Withdraw suit, Admit liability, Immovable buy, Transfer immovable, Enter partnership.

cases.title: Pinnacle Traders: authority, money and a minor
cases.case: Pinnacle Traders, a firm dealing in electrical goods, has partners Quresh, Rhea and Sahil, and Tara, a minor admitted to the benefits. There is no written deed. On 1 August 2025 Rhea advanced ₹1,50,000 to the firm beyond her capital. In December 2025 Quresh, without telling the others, (i) bought 400 fans from a regular supplier on credit in the firm's name and (ii) settled the firm's claim of ₹2,00,000 against a customer for ₹1,20,000. Sahil wants a salary of ₹4,000 per month because he looks after the shop. Tara turned 18 on 15 April 2026; she has always known of her admission and has given no notice so far.

mcqs.q: What interest is Rhea entitled to on her advance for the year ending 31 March 2026?
options: Nil — no agreement exists
mcqs.explain: Section 13(d) gives 6% a year on a partner's advance beyond capital, even without an agreement. Rhea advanced the money on 1 August 2025, so it ran for 8 months to 31 March 2026: ₹1,50,000 × 6% × 8/12 = ₹6,000. ₹9,000 is the trap: it charges a full year. ₹12,000 uses an 8% rate, and "Nil" confuses an advance with capital. In practice: a CA finalising the firm's accounts credits this interest to Rhea's current account and checks that the deed or the Act supports the rate.
mcqs.topic: Relation of Partners to One Another

mcqs.q: Which of Quresh's acts binds the firm without the others' consent?
options: Only the purchase of fans on credit
Only the settlement of the claim
Both acts
Neither act
mcqs.explain: Under Section 19(1), buying stock on credit from a regular supplier is done in the usual way of a firm dealing in electrical goods, so it binds the firm. Section 19(2)(c) denies a partner implied authority to compromise or give up a claim of the firm, so settling ₹2,00,000 for ₹1,20,000 does not bind the firm without the others' consent. "Both acts" is the trap: it ignores that exclusion. In practice: firms often authorise one partner in writing to settle debtor disputes, to avoid challenges later.
mcqs.topic: Relation of Partners to Third Parties

mcqs.q: Is Sahil entitled to the salary he claims?
options: No — Section 13(a) denies remuneration unless agreed
Yes — he works full time
Yes, at 6% of profits
Only if the firm earns a profit
mcqs.explain: Section 13(a): unless agreed, a partner gets no salary or other pay for working in the business. With no written deed, Sahil has no claim to a salary, however much he works. "Yes, he works full time" is the trap: effort does not create a right to pay without agreement. In practice: partners who run the business ask the CA to add a salary clause in the deed, which also lets the firm claim a deduction for it, within the limits set by income-tax law.
mcqs.topic: Relation of Partners to One Another

mcqs.q: If Tara gives no public notice, when does she become a partner?
options: On 15 October 2026, six months after attaining majority
On 15 April 2026
Never, unless she signs a deed
On 15 April 2027
mcqs.explain: Section 30(5): Tara must give public notice within six months of attaining majority or learning of her admission, whichever is later. She always knew, so the period runs from 15 April 2026 and ends on 15 October 2026. If she stays silent, she becomes a partner then, and under Section 30(7) she is liable for all acts of the firm since her admission to benefits. "15 April 2026" is the trap: that only starts the period. In practice: CAs diarise such dates in family firms so that the minor decides in time.
mcqs.topic: Minors Admitted to the Benefits of Partnership (Section 30)
